specAnchors.text: know the definition of standard enthalpy change of: i reaction, ∆ r H ii formation, ∆ f H iii combustion, ∆ c H iv neutralisation, ∆ neut H v atomisation, ∆ at H

primer.text: Five standard enthalpy changes anchor the energetics chapter: reaction, formation, combustion, neutralisation and atomisation. Each definition fixes the substance, the quantity of one mole and the standard conditions. This note states all five, writes the matching equations, and shows why an element in its standard state scores zero.

modules.title: The five standard enthalpy definitions
modules.opening: Five definitions anchor the energetics chapter, and each one hides three marks: the substance, the quantity of one mole, and the standard conditions. Learn them as a family - reaction, formation, combustion, neutralisation and atomisation - and read the precision each demands.
keyPoints: Standard conditions are 100 kPa pressure and 298 K, with every substance in its standard state.
The standard enthalpy change of reaction is the enthalpy change for the equation's stated amounts.
The standard enthalpy change of formation is the change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements.
The standard enthalpy change of combustion is the change when one mole burns completely in oxygen.
Neutralisation gives one mole of water; atomisation gives one mole of gaseous atoms from the element.

low.restatement: Five labels, one template: state the substance, fix the quantity at one mole (except the general reaction change), and pin the standard conditions of 100 kPa and 298 K.
low.analogy: Five passport photos of the same idea: the face (substance) changes, the frame (one mole, standard conditions) never does.
low.examPointer: Losing the word 'standard' or the 'one mole' phrase is how most definition marks die - write both into every definition.

medium.restatement: The definitions are equation-generating machines: formation demands elements in standard states making exactly one mole of product; combustion demands complete oxidation to CO2 and H2O; atomisation demands free gaseous atoms - each constraint writes the equation for you.
medium.analogy: Each definition is a fill-in-the-blank template; the blanks (states, coefficients) are where the marks hide.
medium.examPointer: Write the equation beside the definition when asked - a definition without its balanced equation earns only half the available credit.

modules.title: The definitions table in use
modules.opening: The definitions earn their keep when converted into equations. Two conventions run the table: an element in its standard state carries zero formation enthalpy, and every formation equation balances to exactly one mole of product.
keyPoints: An element in its standard state has a standard enthalpy change of formation of zero.
Formation equations must balance to exactly one mole of the compound on the product side.
Fractional coefficients on the elements are permitted to reach the one-mole target.
Combustion equations send one mole of fuel to CO2 and H2O with states shown.
Reading the definitions table means converting each row into its balanced, state-specified equation.

low.restatement: Elements in their normal state score zero; formation equations balance to one mole of product even if that needs fractions like half a molecule of oxygen.
low.analogy: The zero is the reference floor of the energy ladder, and the one-mole rule is the ladder's fixed rung spacing.
low.examPointer: Do not clear fractions to whole numbers in formation equations - the one-mole product overrides the no-fractions habit from other topics.

medium.restatement: The zero convention exists because the ladder needs a floor: measuring formation relative to elements removes arbitrary absolute energies and makes cycles additive - every later Hess calculation stands on this floor.
medium.analogy: Sea level is the zero for mountains; elements in standard states are the sea level of enthalpy.
medium.examPointer: Write state symbols in every equation from the table - the state symbols are part of the definition's precision and carry marks.

glossary.definition: The reference conditions of 100 kPa and 298 K under which standard enthalpy changes are quoted.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions.
The enthalpy change when one mole of water forms in an acid-base reaction.
